title: Florence Warfield Sillers

encoding_log.content:
Title: Florence Warfield Sillers

Florence Carson Warfield Sillers was an American socialite and historian who became a prominent figure in Mississippi society. She was born on September 25, 1869, in Boonville, Missouri, and spent her childhood in Louisiana and Mississippi. Her parents were Colonel Elisha Warfield and Mary Anderson Carson. Her father was a planter who owned a plantation in Bolivar County, Mississippi, near the town of Rosedale. During the American Civil War he served as a Confederate officer in the 2nd Arkansas Infantry Regiment. Through him, Sillers was connected to a long-established American family with colonial roots. Sillers’s paternal ancestors had emigrated from Great Britain to the Province of Maryland in the seventeenth century. Among her notable relatives was her great-grandfather, also named Elisha Warfield, who was a physician and horse breeder. She was also a grandniece of Mary Jane Warfield Clay, who was known as a suffragist. These family connections linked her both to early colonial settlers and to later political and social activism.

In 1887, at the age of seventeen, Florence Warfield married Walter Sillers, a lawyer and member of a prominent Mississippi Delta family. She was his second wife. The couple had six children: Anna Farrar Sillers, Mary Sillers Skinner, Florence Sillers Ogden, Walter Sillers Jr., Evelyn Sillers Pearson, and Lillian Burrill Sillers Holleman. Her husband owned several plantations in Bolivar County and was active in state politics as a member of the Mississippi Democratic executive committee. The family lived in a Victorian-style mansion on Levee Street in Rosedale, Mississippi, which served as a base for their social and civic activities.

As a leading society figure in Mississippi, Florence Warfield Sillers belonged to numerous social, civic, and lineage organizations. She participated in local chapters of the Colonial Dames of America, an organization for women descended from prominent figures in the American colonies. She was also involved with the American Farm Bureau Federation and the American Red Cross, reflecting her interests in agriculture and public service. In addition, she took part in the activities of the Mississippi Delta Council and the Rosedale Country Club, groups that brought together influential residents of the region.

Religion and philanthropy played an important role in her public life. Sillers was a member of the Methodist Episcopal Church and devoted considerable time to charitable work. For twenty years she served as treasurer of the King’s Daughters Hospital of Rosedale, handling financial matters for the institution. Her historical interests were reflected in her membership in both the Texas State Historical Association and the Mississippi Historical Society, indicating her engagement with regional and state history beyond purely social pursuits.

A significant part of her identity was tied to lineage and historical societies. She was a founding member of the Mississippi Delta Chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution, an organization for women descended from individuals who contributed to American independence. Within this chapter she later served as regent, a leadership role responsible for guiding the group’s activities. She also joined the National Society Magna Charta Dames and Barons, an association for descendants of signers of the Magna Carta, further emphasizing her interest in hereditary connections to historical events and figures.

Sillers became known not only as a socialite but also as a writer of local history. In 1948 she published a book titled "History of Bolivar County, Mississippi." This work examined the history of Bolivar County but did so from a perspective that glorified the Confederacy and idealized the antebellum South. The book contributed to the Lost Cause narrative, a view of the Civil War and the Confederacy that sought to portray the Southern cause in a sympathetic and romanticized light.

Florence Carson Warfield Sillers lived until April 5, 1958, when she died in Mississippi. She was buried in Beulah Cemetery in Beulah, Mississippi. Over the course of her long life, she combined the roles of planter’s daughter, plantation owner’s wife, mother of six children, society leader, and amateur historian. Her many affiliations with historical, civic, and lineage societies, her prominent place in Mississippi social circles, and her authorship of a county history that promoted the Lost Cause interpretation of the Civil War together define her historical legacy as a representative of elite white Southern culture in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

Title: Facebook, Inc. v. Duguid

Facebook, Inc. v. Duguid, 592 U.S. ___ (2021), was a United States Supreme Court case concerning how to interpret the term "automatic telephone dialing system" under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act of 1991 (TCPA). The dispute arose over whether Facebook’s security-alert text messaging system qualified as an autodialer under the statute and thus could expose the company to liability for sending unsolicited text messages.

The TCPA was enacted in 1991 to reduce the growing number of unsolicited calls consumers were receiving. Among its provisions, the law restricted the use of automated telephone dialing systems, often called autodialers, to contact consumers on services that might cost the recipient money, including cell phones and text messaging. Violations of these restrictions could be investigated and fined by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC).

Over time, Congress amended the TCPA. One important amendment, adopted in 2015, created an exception that allowed automated calls to numbers associated with services that charge the called party, when those calls were made to collect debts owed to or guaranteed by the federal government.

Since the law’s enactment, the TCPA’s autodialer restrictions have been challenged on First Amendment grounds, with plaintiffs arguing that the statute impermissibly restricted speech. Federal courts of appeals generally upheld the statute, finding it consistent with free speech protections.

The 2015 amendment, however, introduced a new constitutional argument. By exempting automated calls for federal debt collection, the law appeared to favor one type of speech over others, potentially making the autodialer restriction a content-based regulation of speech and therefore more vulnerable under the First Amendment.

At the same time that Facebook, Inc. v. Duguid was proceeding, another case, Barr v. American Association of Political Consultants, Inc., was advancing toward the Supreme Court to address whether this 2015 amendment rendered the autodialer provisions unconstitutional.

The factual dispute in Facebook, Inc. v. Duguid began in 2014, when Noah Duguid started receiving text messages on his cell phone from Facebook. These messages warned him of suspicious activity on a Facebook account, but Duguid did not have a Facebook account at all.

After attempting unsuccessfully to get Facebook to stop the messages, Duguid filed a class-action lawsuit in March 2015 in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California. He alleged that Facebook had violated the TCPA’s autodialer provision by using an automatic telephone dialing system (ATDS) to send him unwanted text messages.

Facebook moved to dismiss the lawsuit on two main grounds. First, it argued that its login or security notification system was not an ATDS because it did not generate phone numbers randomly or sequentially; instead, it sent targeted messages to specific numbers associated with particular user accounts or entries in a database. Second, Facebook challenged the constitutionality of the TCPA’s autodialer provision as modified by the 2015 amendment, contending that the law had become a content-based restriction on speech that violated the First Amendment.

Because the case now raised a constitutional question, the federal government intervened to defend the TCPA and support dismissal.

The district court ruled in Facebook’s favor and dismissed Duguid’s complaint. The court concluded that Duguid had not adequately alleged that Facebook’s system qualified as an ATDS under the statutory definition, which referred to equipment that could store or produce telephone numbers using a random or sequential number generator.

Duguid appealed to the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. On appeal, Facebook again argued that its notification system did not meet the statutory definition of an ATDS, and the federal government again appeared to defend the TCPA.

title: Tamuri Wigness

encoding_log.content:
Title: Tamuri Wigness

Tamuri Slim Wigness Jr., born on 26 March 2002, is an Australian professional basketball player who most recently played for the North Gold Coast Seahawks in the NBL1 North. He was born in the Torres Strait Islands region of Queensland, Australia, and is of Indigenous Australian (Muralag) heritage.

At an early age, he moved with his family to Cairns, Queensland, where he began his primary schooling. While living in Cairns, his first sporting interest was junior rugby league, which he played until the age of 10. His mother then suggested he switch to basketball because it involved less physical contact, and he followed her advice.

Within a year of taking up basketball, Wigness joined Cairns Basketball's Tiny Taipans development program, which provided structured training and exposure to higher levels of the sport. At just 11 years old, he was given the opportunity to train with professional players from the Cairns Taipans, a National Basketball League (NBL) team.

During his teenage years, he attended Cairns State High School. While in high school, he continued to develop as a basketball player but also played junior Australian rules football with the Manunda Hawks in the local AFL Cairns competition. His performances in Australian rules football led to selection in multiple junior representative teams.

As a promising dual-sport athlete, Wigness drew interest from professional talent scouts. Along with fellow Cairns junior basketball standout Alex Davies, he was scouted by the Gold Coast Suns, an Australian Football League (AFL) club. Both players were offered places in the Suns' developmental academy. Davies accepted the offer and pursued a career in football, while Wigness chose to focus on basketball, declining the AFL pathway. Despite their different sporting directions, the two remained close friends and often trained together in both sports when they were based in the same area.

Wigness emerged as a leading junior basketball player in Queensland. At 14 years of age, he represented Queensland at the 2016 under-16 national championships. He starred throughout the tournament, averaging 25.56 points per game, and produced a standout performance by scoring 45 points in a game against South Australia.

In 2017, he accepted an NBA Global Academy scholarship, which granted him access to first-class training facilities at the Australian Institute of Sport complex in Canberra. That same year, he again represented Queensland at the under-16 national championships. His dominant play at state level led to his selection for the Australian national team at the 2017 FIBA Under-16 Asian Championship. There, he played a pivotal role in helping Australia win the gold medal and was named the starting point guard in the tournament's All-Tournament Team.

In 2018, Wigness travelled to Treviso, Italy, to participate in the NBA Global Camp. At this event, he impressed international scouts, forming an athletic backcourt combination with fellow Australian guard Josh Green.

Wigness continued to represent Australia in junior international competitions. He was part of the gold medal-winning Australian teams at the 2018 FIBA Under-18 Asian Championship and the 2019 FIBA Oceania Under-18 Championship. He also competed for Australia at the 2018 FIBA Under-17 Basketball World Cup and the 2019 FIBA Under-19 Basketball World Cup.

From 2017 to 2020, Wigness attended and played for the Basketball Australia Centre of Excellence, competing in the SEABL, NBL1, and Waratah League. During the 2019 NBL1 season, he averaged 11.7 points, four assists, and 3.4 rebounds per game, and in his season finale he recorded 22 points and 12 assists.

In 2019 he also travelled to Charlotte, North Carolina, to compete in the Basketball Without Borders Global Camp, where he again caught the attention of college and NBA scouts and earned All-Tournament honours.

title: Queer art

encoding_log.content:
Title: Queer art

Queer art, also known as LGBT+ art or queer aesthetics, broadly refers to modern and contemporary visual art practices that draw on lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and other non-heterosexual or non-cisgender imagery and issues. By definition there can be no single, unified category of "queer art", because it encompasses a wide range of identities, contexts, and artistic approaches. 

However, contemporary artists who identify their practices as queer often call upon utopian and dystopian alternatives to ordinary life, adopt outlaw stances, embrace criminality and opacity, and forge unprecedented kinships and relationships. Queer art can be explicitly about sex and the embracing of unauthorised desires, challenging norms around sexuality and gender. Queer art is highly site-specific, with practices emerging very differently depending on context. 

In some places, queer artistic expression is advocated for and celebrated, while in others it is met with backlash, censorship, or even criminalisation. Because sex and gender operate differently in various national, religious, and ethnic contexts, queer art necessarily takes on varied meanings across cultures. Historically, the term "queer" functioned as a homophobic slur, particularly visible during the AIDS crisis in the United States in the 1980s. Since then, it has been re-appropriated and embraced by queer activists and integrated into many English-speaking academic and cultural contexts. 

As a result, international art practices by LGBT+ individuals are often placed under the umbrella term "queer art" in English-language discourse, even when they emerge outside the specific historical developments of U.S. gender and identity politics from the 1980s. The label "queer art" has also been used retroactively to describe the historic work of LGBT+ artists who practiced before present-day terminology such as lesbian, gay, bisexual, and trans was recognised. An example is the 2017 Tate exhibition "Queer British Art 1861–1967", which gathered works by artists whose lives and themes are now read through queer perspectives. 

The term "queer" is situated in the politics of non-normative gay, lesbian, and bisexual communities, though it is not equivalent to any of these categories and remains a fluid identity. Queer art adheres to no particular style or medium. It can take the form of performance art, video art, installation, drawing, painting, sculpture, photography, film, glass, and mixed media, among many other formats. 

Art historian Alex Pilcher, in "A Queer Little History of Art", notes that across art history, biographical information about queer artists has often been omitted or downplayed, or interpreted under the assumption of heterosexual identity. Same-sex partners might be described merely as "close friends", and artistic comrades recast as heterosexual love interests. Gay artists have historically been diagnosed in the record as celibate, asexual, or sexually confused, obscuring the queer dimensions of their lives and work. 

During the interwar period, there was greater acceptance of queer individuals in certain artistic urban centres such as Paris and Berlin. In 1920s New York, speakeasies in Harlem and Greenwich Village welcomed gay and lesbian clients, and cafés and bars across Europe and Latin America hosted artistic groups in which gay men could be integrated into mainstream cultural developments. Even in these more permissive environments, artists often developed visual codes to signify queerness covertly. 

Art historian Jonathan David Katz has written about Agnes Martin's abstract paintings as a form of queer self-realisation, suggesting that the tense, unreconciled equilibrium in works such as "Night Sea" (1963) reflects her identity as a closeted lesbian. Katz has also interpreted the iconography in Robert Rauschenberg's combine paintings, such as the inclusion of a picture of Judy Garland in "Bantam" (1954) and references to the myth of Ganymede in "Canyon" (1959), as allusions to Rauschenberg's identity as a gay man. 

Considering Rauschenberg's relationship with Jasper Johns, art historian Andrew Graham-Dixon reads Johns's monochrome encaustic painting "White Flag" (1955) in relation to Johns's experiences as a gay man in a repressive American society.

title: Queer art

encoding_log.content:
Title: Queer art

Queer art, also known as LGBT+ art or queer aesthetics, broadly refers to modern and contemporary visual art practices that draw on lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and other non-heterosexual or non-cisgender imagery and issues. By definition there can be no single, unified category of "queer art", because it encompasses a wide range of identities, contexts, and artistic approaches. 

However, contemporary artists who identify their practices as queer often call upon utopian and dystopian alternatives to ordinary life, adopt outlaw stances, embrace criminality and opacity, and forge unprecedented kinships and relationships. Queer art can be explicitly about sex and the embracing of unauthorised desires, challenging norms around sexuality and gender. Queer art is highly site-specific, with practices emerging very differently depending on context. 

In some places, queer artistic expression is advocated for and celebrated, while in others it is met with backlash, censorship, or even criminalisation. Because sex and gender operate differently in various national, religious, and ethnic contexts, queer art necessarily takes on varied meanings across cultures. Historically, the term "queer" functioned as a homophobic slur, particularly visible during the AIDS crisis in the United States in the 1980s. Since then, it has been re-appropriated and embraced by queer activists and integrated into many English-speaking academic and cultural contexts. 

As a result, international art practices by LGBT+ individuals are often placed under the umbrella term "queer art" in English-language discourse, even when they emerge outside the specific historical developments of U.S. gender and identity politics from the 1980s. The label "queer art" has also been used retroactively to describe the historic work of LGBT+ artists who practiced before present-day terminology such as lesbian, gay, bisexual, and trans was recognised. An example is the 2017 Tate exhibition "Queer British Art 1861–1967", which gathered works by artists whose lives and themes are now read through queer perspectives. 

The term "queer" is situated in the politics of non-normative gay, lesbian, and bisexual communities, though it is not equivalent to any of these categories and remains a fluid identity. Queer art adheres to no particular style or medium. It can take the form of performance art, video art, installation, drawing, painting, sculpture, photography, film, glass, and mixed media, among many other formats. 

Art historian Alex Pilcher, in "A Queer Little History of Art", notes that across art history, biographical information about queer artists has often been omitted or downplayed, or interpreted under the assumption of heterosexual identity. Same-sex partners might be described merely as "close friends", and artistic comrades recast as heterosexual love interests. Gay artists have historically been diagnosed in the record as celibate, asexual, or sexually confused, obscuring the queer dimensions of their lives and work. 

During the interwar period, there was greater acceptance of queer individuals in certain artistic urban centres such as Paris and Berlin. In 1920s New York, speakeasies in Harlem and Greenwich Village welcomed gay and lesbian clients, and cafés and bars across Europe and Latin America hosted artistic groups in which gay men could be integrated into mainstream cultural developments. Even in these more permissive environments, artists often developed visual codes to signify queerness covertly. 

Art historian Jonathan David Katz has written about Agnes Martin's abstract paintings as a form of queer self-realisation, suggesting that the tense, unreconciled equilibrium in works such as "Night Sea" (1963) reflects her identity as a closeted lesbian. Katz has also interpreted the iconography in Robert Rauschenberg's combine paintings, such as the inclusion of a picture of Judy Garland in "Bantam" (1954) and references to the myth of Ganymede in "Canyon" (1959), as allusions to Rauschenberg's identity as a gay man. 

Considering Rauschenberg's relationship with Jasper Johns, art historian Andrew Graham-Dixon reads Johns's monochrome encaustic painting "White Flag" (1955) in relation to Johns's experiences as a gay man in a repressive American society.

title: Florence Warfield Sillers

encoding_log.content:
Title: Florence Warfield Sillers

Florence Carson Warfield Sillers was an American socialite and historian who became a prominent figure in Mississippi society. She was born on September 25, 1869, in Boonville, Missouri, and spent her childhood in Louisiana and Mississippi. Her parents were Colonel Elisha Warfield and Mary Anderson Carson. Her father was a planter who owned a plantation in Bolivar County, Mississippi, near the town of Rosedale. During the American Civil War he served as a Confederate officer in the 2nd Arkansas Infantry Regiment. Through him, Sillers was connected to a long-established American family with colonial roots. Sillers’s paternal ancestors had emigrated from Great Britain to the Province of Maryland in the seventeenth century. Among her notable relatives was her great-grandfather, also named Elisha Warfield, who was a physician and horse breeder. She was also a grandniece of Mary Jane Warfield Clay, who was known as a suffragist. These family connections linked her both to early colonial settlers and to later political and social activism.

In 1887, at the age of seventeen, Florence Warfield married Walter Sillers, a lawyer and member of a prominent Mississippi Delta family. She was his second wife. The couple had six children: Anna Farrar Sillers, Mary Sillers Skinner, Florence Sillers Ogden, Walter Sillers Jr., Evelyn Sillers Pearson, and Lillian Burrill Sillers Holleman. Her husband owned several plantations in Bolivar County and was active in state politics as a member of the Mississippi Democratic executive committee. The family lived in a Victorian-style mansion on Levee Street in Rosedale, Mississippi, which served as a base for their social and civic activities.

As a leading society figure in Mississippi, Florence Warfield Sillers belonged to numerous social, civic, and lineage organizations. She participated in local chapters of the Colonial Dames of America, an organization for women descended from prominent figures in the American colonies. She was also involved with the American Farm Bureau Federation and the American Red Cross, reflecting her interests in agriculture and public service. In addition, she took part in the activities of the Mississippi Delta Council and the Rosedale Country Club, groups that brought together influential residents of the region.

Religion and philanthropy played an important role in her public life. Sillers was a member of the Methodist Episcopal Church and devoted considerable time to charitable work. For twenty years she served as treasurer of the King’s Daughters Hospital of Rosedale, handling financial matters for the institution. Her historical interests were reflected in her membership in both the Texas State Historical Association and the Mississippi Historical Society, indicating her engagement with regional and state history beyond purely social pursuits.

A significant part of her identity was tied to lineage and historical societies. She was a founding member of the Mississippi Delta Chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution, an organization for women descended from individuals who contributed to American independence. Within this chapter she later served as regent, a leadership role responsible for guiding the group’s activities. She also joined the National Society Magna Charta Dames and Barons, an association for descendants of signers of the Magna Carta, further emphasizing her interest in hereditary connections to historical events and figures.

Sillers became known not only as a socialite but also as a writer of local history. In 1948 she published a book titled "History of Bolivar County, Mississippi." This work examined the history of Bolivar County but did so from a perspective that glorified the Confederacy and idealized the antebellum South. The book contributed to the Lost Cause narrative, a view of the Civil War and the Confederacy that sought to portray the Southern cause in a sympathetic and romanticized light.

Florence Carson Warfield Sillers lived until April 5, 1958, when she died in Mississippi. She was buried in Beulah Cemetery in Beulah, Mississippi. Over the course of her long life, she combined the roles of planter’s daughter, plantation owner’s wife, mother of six children, society leader, and amateur historian. Her many affiliations with historical, civic, and lineage societies, her prominent place in Mississippi social circles, and her authorship of a county history that promoted the Lost Cause interpretation of the Civil War together define her historical legacy as a representative of elite white Southern culture in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

title: Luce Turnier

encoding_log.content:
Title: Luce Turnier

Luce Turnier (February 24, 1924 – 1994) was a Haitian painter and collage artist who became one of Haiti’s leading modernist figures. She was born in 1924 in Jacmel, a town in southern Haiti. In 1937 a devastating hurricane struck southern Haiti, prompting her family to relocate to the capital, Port-au-Prince. This move later proved important for her artistic development, as Port-au-Prince became the center of a growing Haitian art movement.

Turnier began painting in 1944, at the age of 21, when she enrolled at Le Centre d’Art in Port-au-Prince. She soon became one of the founding members of this art school and gallery, which would play a central role in the emergence of modern Haitian art. As a young artist she admired the work of Brazilian painter Cândido Portinari and German artist Käthe Kollwitz, though she later explained that she grew out of these early influences as she developed her own style.

In a 1983 interview, Turnier described her training at Le Centre d’Art, noting that students started with still life and figure drawing, working from nude models and arranged objects. On Saturdays they went outdoors to paint landscapes, giving students a range of both studio and open-air experience.

Turnier belonged to Haiti’s middle class, as did Marie-Josée Nadal and Rose-Marie Desruisseaux, the other founding female artists at Le Centre d’Art. Their social status gave them access to artistic education, but middle-class Haitian society of the time did not encourage women to pursue careers in the arts. Women who persisted in artistic work were often stigmatized as deviants. Turnier recalled that although many women visited the Centre for a class or two, only about four or five women attended regularly in those early years. She also remembered the disdainful attitude of the Haitian bourgeoisie, who initially regarded the Centre’s artists as if they were “hippies” or “punks.”

Her paintings were featured in Studio No. 3, Le Centre d’Art’s monthly magazine. Turnier and a constellation of associated artists, including Albert Mangonès, Gérald Bloncourt, Maurice Borno, Rigaud Benoit, Hector Hyppolite, Daniel Lafontant, and others, formed the core of what became known as the Haitian Art Movement. The period from 1946 to 1950, which overlapped with the early phase of her career, is sometimes called “The Haitian Renaissance,” reflecting the vitality and innovation of Haitian visual arts at the time.

In 1946, with support from UNESCO, Turnier’s works were exhibited at the Musée d’Art Moderne de Paris, signaling her early international recognition. From December 8, 1949 until June 1950, her "Self-Portrait" was shown in the fine arts pavilion at the International Bi-Centennial Celebration of Port-au-Prince. In 1950 she and fellow artist Lucien Price helped to found an art gallery called The Foyer, further strengthening the institutional base for Haitian artists.

During the early 1950s, both the French and Haitian governments awarded Turnier scholarships to study abroad in the United States and Europe. She exhibited her work in Europe and studied in New York City and Paris. In New York she attended the Art Students League, where she became immersed in modernist theory that rejected traditional spatial illusionism and insisted on preserving the flatness of the picture plane.

Throughout this period she struggled to develop a personal style that integrated her Haitian heritage without surrendering to market expectations about what Haitian art should look like. She resisted stereotypical images favored by collectors who wanted exotic or folkloric themes, such as overt references to Haitian folklore and Vodou.

Turnier’s personal life intersected with her artistic trajectory. In 1954 she married the Italian painter Eugenio Carpi de Resmini, and the couple had two children. In 1965 she remarried, this time to the French painter Christian Lemesle.

title: Skeleton Coast (film)

encoding_log.content:
Title: Skeleton Coast (film)

Skeleton Coast is a 1987 South African mercenary war film directed by John Cardos. It was the first of three films Cardos made for producer Harry Alan Towers and also the first production of Towers' company, Breton Film Productions. The film is set during the Angolan Civil War and follows a rescue mission led by a retired American military officer.

The story begins with CIA agent Michael Smith, who is working with UNITA rebels in Angola. During his activities with the rebels, he is captured by the Angolan Armed Forces. After his capture, Michael is taken to a prison where he is interrogated by an East German officer, Major Schneider.

Michael's father, Colonel Bill Smith, is a retired officer of the United States Marine Corps. When the Colonel learns of his son's capture, he loses faith in the ability or willingness of the United States Government to secure Michael's release through official channels. Determined to rescue his son by himself, Colonel Smith travels to South West Africa. There he seeks information about Michael's whereabouts and negotiates with a mysterious local figure named Elia, paying him for accurate intelligence on the location of the prison where his son is being held.

After obtaining this information, the Colonel organizes a private rescue mission. He hires seven mercenaries and takes command of this small force, planning to cross into Angola and free Michael. Complications develop around a diamond mine in the region. Captain David Simpson, who is in charge of security for the diamond mine, becomes suspicious of Colonel Smith's activities. Fearing that the Colonel might be involved in diamond smuggling rather than a rescue mission, Simpson orders one of his men to keep the Colonel under surveillance.

At the same time, Simpson maintains an illicit relationship with Elia's wife, Opal. When one of Simpson's security men is killed, Opal falsely tells Simpson that Colonel Smith murdered the man. In reality, the killing was carried out by Rick Weston, the leader of the mercenary group hired by the Colonel. Rick Weston tells Colonel Smith that he himself is an Angolan secret agent, adding another layer of deception.

Meanwhile, Elia discovers a financial betrayal. After being paid by Colonel Smith, he later finds that the money stored in his safe has been replaced with counterfeit currency, or that it had been counterfeit from the start. This discovery further undermines the fragile trust among the characters.

As the mercenary team moves into Angola, they form an alliance with Sekassi, a rebel leader comparable to Jonas Savimbi, the well-known head of UNITA. Sekassi and his rebels join forces with the mercenaries to support the mission to rescue Michael Smith from captivity.

The film features an international cast. Ernest Borgnine plays Colonel Bill Smith, the determined father leading the rescue mission. Robert Vaughn portrays Major Schneider, the East German interrogator of Michael Smith. Oliver Reed appears as Captain David Simpson, responsible for the diamond mine's security. Herbert Lom plays Elia, the enigmatic figure who sells information to the Colonel. Daniel Greene appears as Rick Weston, the head of the hired mercenaries, while Leon Isaac Kennedy plays a character named Chuck. Nancy Mulford portrays Sam, and Peter Kwong plays Tohsiro. Robin Townsend takes the role of Opal, Elia's unfaithful wife. Simon Sabela appears as Sekassi, the rebel leader, with Arnold Vosloo as Blade, Tullio Moneta as Armando, Larry Taylor as Robbins, and Jonathan Rands as Michael Smith.

Behind the scenes, Nadia Caillou, daughter of screenwriter and author Alan Caillou, made her screenwriting debut on Skeleton Coast. Alan Caillou was known for his "Private Army of Colonel Tobin" series of novels.

title: Nobody's Love

encoding_log.content:
Title: Nobody's Love

"Nobody's Love" is a song by the American band Maroon 5, released through 222 and Interscope Records on July 24, 2020. It served as the second single from the band’s seventh studio album, titled "Jordi." The track is notable in the group’s discography as their first single released without longtime bassist Mickey Madden. The timing and themes of the song closely reflect the events of 2020, as it was inspired by both the COVID-19 pandemic and the widespread protests that followed the killing of George Floyd in the United States.

Commercially, "Nobody's Love" had a mixed chart performance. On the Billboard Hot 100, it peaked at number 41. This made it the band’s first single since "Feelings" in 2015 to miss the Top 40 of that chart, a relative underperformance compared to many of their previous hits. However, the song was more successful on Billboard’s Adult Top 40 chart, where it became Maroon 5’s seventh consecutive top-ten hit and their record-extending twenty-sixth top-ten entry overall, demonstrating the band’s enduring popularity on adult contemporary and pop radio formats.

A remix of "Nobody's Love" was later released, expanding the song’s reach and stylistic palette. This version, a collaboration with Jamaican singer-songwriter Popcaan, came out on October 16, 2020. The remix kept the core structure of the original but introduced Popcaan’s distinctive vocal style and a subtle reggae and dancehall influence, providing an alternative take on the song while maintaining its emotional themes.

The release of "Nobody's Love" was announced a few days before it became available. On July 20, 2020, Maroon 5 revealed that the single would be released at midnight on July 24. At the same time, the band unveiled its cover art. The artwork features a vivid, colorful image depicting a woman looking out at the ocean, rendered in a mysterious and stylized manner. There are three different versions of this cover, all created in Technicolor and incorporating a Smiley face logo, which contributes to the visual identity associated with the single.

Frontman Adam Levine explained the song’s inspiration and intended message in the context of 2020’s global crises. He stated that the process of perfecting "Nobody's Love" was undertaken with the entire world in mind. Levine expressed the hope that the song would offer listeners a moment of peace and reflection during an unprecedented period marked by a global pandemic and intense social unrest. He dedicated the song broadly to essential workers on the front lines of the health crisis, to citizens actively engaged in the fight for social justice, and to anyone needing a reminder of what he called the potent power of love.

The music video for "Nobody's Love" premiered on YouTube at midnight Eastern Time, coinciding with the song’s release. Directed by David Dobkin, a frequent Maroon 5 collaborator, the video was shot in isolation in Los Angeles, California, during pandemic-related restrictions. Unusually for a major pop release, it was filmed entirely on an Apple iPhone. The video presents a solitary Adam Levine sitting in a wooden chair in a backyard at night, smoking a marijuana cigarette. Its stripped-down, intimate setting underscores the themes of isolation and contemplation.

In conjunction with the video, Maroon 5 partnered with the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), issuing a joint letter that framed the imagery and release within ongoing conversations about civil rights and social justice.

A separate lyric video for "Nobody's Love" was released on August 26, 2020. This visual presentation echoed the single’s cover art, employing a color-changing aesthetic with soothing images of waves crashing against the coastline. The combination of shifting colors and calm ocean scenes was designed to complement the song’s reflective tone and reinforce its message of solace.

title: Mykhailo Radutskyi

encoding_log.content:
Title: Mykhailo Radutskyi

Mykhailo Borysovych Radutskyi is a Ukrainian entrepreneur, social activist, and politician who has served as a People's Deputy of Ukraine in multiple convocations of the Verkhovna Rada, the country’s national parliament. He was born on 5 December 1968 in Kyiv, the capital of Ukraine. His educational background combines medical training and sports science. Radutskyi studied at the P. I. Gavros Kyiv Medical College, where he qualified as an Emergency Medical Technician. He later continued his education at the National University of Ukraine on Physical Education and Sport, specializing in Olympic and professional sport. At this institution he received a master’s degree in Olympic and professional sport.

Early in his career Radutskyi worked directly in the medical field. In 1987 he served as an Emergency Medical Technician at a Kyiv ambulance station, applying his medical college training to emergency healthcare. After this period in frontline medical service, his professional path shifted toward management and the cultural sector. From 1989 to 1993 he held the position of deputy director of an organization called "Kyivconcert." This role marked the beginning of his experience in administration and leadership.

In 1993 Radutskyi entered the medical business. Over the following decade he built a career as a manager in a private medical company. From 1994 to 2004 he served as commercial director and then deputy director of the limited liability company "Boris." In 2004 he became president of LLC "Boris," reflecting his growing influence and responsibility in the private healthcare sector. His work there connected his early medical training with entrepreneurial activity and healthcare management.

Radutskyi also became active in broader medical governance. At some point he was a member of the Higher Medical Council of the Ministry of Healthcare of Ukraine, indicating his involvement in national-level medical policy or advisory work. His role extended beyond the private sector into public and professional health structures.

In 2015 he moved further into public service when he became an advisor to the head of the Kyiv City State Administration, Vitali Klitschko. This advisory role placed him in the municipal executive sphere of Ukraine’s capital city.

By 2019 Radutskyi had become an important figure in national politics. He was nominated as a candidate for People’s Deputy from the political party Servant of the People for the 2019 parliamentary elections. He appeared as number 18 on the party list, indicating a high position among the party’s candidates, although he himself was formally non-partisan and not a registered member of any party.

On 30 July 2019 President Volodymyr Zelensky appointed him as an out-of-state advisor to the president, further demonstrating the trust placed in him by the country’s leadership.

In the 2019 Ukrainian parliamentary elections Radutskyi was elected a People’s Deputy of Ukraine of the ninth convocation as number 18 on the Servant of the People party list. In parliament he joined the Servant of the People parliamentary faction. Within the Verkhovna Rada he took on a key committee role as Chairperson of the Committee on Public Health, Medical Assistance and Medical Insurance, aligning his legislative work with his professional experience in healthcare.

Radutskyi also became active in interparliamentary cooperation. He served as a member of the Ukrainian part of the interparliamentary assembly that includes the parliament of Georgia, the parliament of the Republic of Moldova, and the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine. In addition, he was a deputy member of the Ukrainian part of the Parliamentary Association Committee.

He headed several groups for inter-parliamentary relations, including those with the Kingdom of Thailand and with the Republic of Moldova. He was also head of a group for inter-parliamentary relations with Moldova, and a member of groups maintaining relations with the Italian Republic, the Republic of Kazakhstan, the Republic of Armenia, the French Republic, and the Republic of Croatia.

title: Florence Warfield Sillers

encoding_log.content:
Title: Florence Warfield Sillers

Florence Carson Warfield Sillers was an American socialite and historian who became a prominent figure in Mississippi society. She was born on September 25, 1869, in Boonville, Missouri, and spent her childhood in Louisiana and Mississippi. Her parents were Colonel Elisha Warfield and Mary Anderson Carson. Her father was a planter who owned a plantation in Bolivar County, Mississippi, near the town of Rosedale. During the American Civil War he served as a Confederate officer in the 2nd Arkansas Infantry Regiment. Through him, Sillers was connected to a long-established American family with colonial roots. Sillers’s paternal ancestors had emigrated from Great Britain to the Province of Maryland in the seventeenth century. Among her notable relatives was her great-grandfather, also named Elisha Warfield, who was a physician and horse breeder. She was also a grandniece of Mary Jane Warfield Clay, who was known as a suffragist. These family connections linked her both to early colonial settlers and to later political and social activism.

In 1887, at the age of seventeen, Florence Warfield married Walter Sillers, a lawyer and member of a prominent Mississippi Delta family. She was his second wife. The couple had six children: Anna Farrar Sillers, Mary Sillers Skinner, Florence Sillers Ogden, Walter Sillers Jr., Evelyn Sillers Pearson, and Lillian Burrill Sillers Holleman. Her husband owned several plantations in Bolivar County and was active in state politics as a member of the Mississippi Democratic executive committee. The family lived in a Victorian-style mansion on Levee Street in Rosedale, Mississippi, which served as a base for their social and civic activities.

As a leading society figure in Mississippi, Florence Warfield Sillers belonged to numerous social, civic, and lineage organizations. She participated in local chapters of the Colonial Dames of America, an organization for women descended from prominent figures in the American colonies. She was also involved with the American Farm Bureau Federation and the American Red Cross, reflecting her interests in agriculture and public service. In addition, she took part in the activities of the Mississippi Delta Council and the Rosedale Country Club, groups that brought together influential residents of the region.

Religion and philanthropy played an important role in her public life. Sillers was a member of the Methodist Episcopal Church and devoted considerable time to charitable work. For twenty years she served as treasurer of the King’s Daughters Hospital of Rosedale, handling financial matters for the institution. Her historical interests were reflected in her membership in both the Texas State Historical Association and the Mississippi Historical Society, indicating her engagement with regional and state history beyond purely social pursuits.

A significant part of her identity was tied to lineage and historical societies. She was a founding member of the Mississippi Delta Chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution, an organization for women descended from individuals who contributed to American independence. Within this chapter she later served as regent, a leadership role responsible for guiding the group’s activities. She also joined the National Society Magna Charta Dames and Barons, an association for descendants of signers of the Magna Carta, further emphasizing her interest in hereditary connections to historical events and figures.

Sillers became known not only as a socialite but also as a writer of local history. In 1948 she published a book titled "History of Bolivar County, Mississippi." This work examined the history of Bolivar County but did so from a perspective that glorified the Confederacy and idealized the antebellum South. The book contributed to the Lost Cause narrative, a view of the Civil War and the Confederacy that sought to portray the Southern cause in a sympathetic and romanticized light.

Florence Carson Warfield Sillers lived until April 5, 1958, when she died in Mississippi. She was buried in Beulah Cemetery in Beulah, Mississippi. Over the course of her long life, she combined the roles of planter’s daughter, plantation owner’s wife, mother of six children, society leader, and amateur historian. Her many affiliations with historical, civic, and lineage societies, her prominent place in Mississippi social circles, and her authorship of a county history that promoted the Lost Cause interpretation of the Civil War together define her historical legacy as a representative of elite white Southern culture in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

title: Luce Turnier

encoding_log.content:
Title: Luce Turnier

Luce Turnier (February 24, 1924 – 1994) was a Haitian painter and collage artist who became one of Haiti’s leading modernist figures. She was born in 1924 in Jacmel, a town in southern Haiti. In 1937 a devastating hurricane struck southern Haiti, prompting her family to relocate to the capital, Port-au-Prince. This move later proved important for her artistic development, as Port-au-Prince became the center of a growing Haitian art movement.

Turnier began painting in 1944, at the age of 21, when she enrolled at Le Centre d’Art in Port-au-Prince. She soon became one of the founding members of this art school and gallery, which would play a central role in the emergence of modern Haitian art. As a young artist she admired the work of Brazilian painter Cândido Portinari and German artist Käthe Kollwitz, though she later explained that she grew out of these early influences as she developed her own style.

In a 1983 interview, Turnier described her training at Le Centre d’Art, noting that students started with still life and figure drawing, working from nude models and arranged objects. On Saturdays they went outdoors to paint landscapes, giving students a range of both studio and open-air experience.

Turnier belonged to Haiti’s middle class, as did Marie-Josée Nadal and Rose-Marie Desruisseaux, the other founding female artists at Le Centre d’Art. Their social status gave them access to artistic education, but middle-class Haitian society of the time did not encourage women to pursue careers in the arts. Women who persisted in artistic work were often stigmatized as deviants. Turnier recalled that although many women visited the Centre for a class or two, only about four or five women attended regularly in those early years. She also remembered the disdainful attitude of the Haitian bourgeoisie, who initially regarded the Centre’s artists as if they were “hippies” or “punks.”

Her paintings were featured in Studio No. 3, Le Centre d’Art’s monthly magazine. Turnier and a constellation of associated artists, including Albert Mangonès, Gérald Bloncourt, Maurice Borno, Rigaud Benoit, Hector Hyppolite, Daniel Lafontant, and others, formed the core of what became known as the Haitian Art Movement. The period from 1946 to 1950, which overlapped with the early phase of her career, is sometimes called “The Haitian Renaissance,” reflecting the vitality and innovation of Haitian visual arts at the time.

In 1946, with support from UNESCO, Turnier’s works were exhibited at the Musée d’Art Moderne de Paris, signaling her early international recognition. From December 8, 1949 until June 1950, her "Self-Portrait" was shown in the fine arts pavilion at the International Bi-Centennial Celebration of Port-au-Prince. In 1950 she and fellow artist Lucien Price helped to found an art gallery called The Foyer, further strengthening the institutional base for Haitian artists.

During the early 1950s, both the French and Haitian governments awarded Turnier scholarships to study abroad in the United States and Europe. She exhibited her work in Europe and studied in New York City and Paris. In New York she attended the Art Students League, where she became immersed in modernist theory that rejected traditional spatial illusionism and insisted on preserving the flatness of the picture plane.

Throughout this period she struggled to develop a personal style that integrated her Haitian heritage without surrendering to market expectations about what Haitian art should look like. She resisted stereotypical images favored by collectors who wanted exotic or folkloric themes, such as overt references to Haitian folklore and Vodou.

Turnier’s personal life intersected with her artistic trajectory. In 1954 she married the Italian painter Eugenio Carpi de Resmini, and the couple had two children. In 1965 she remarried, this time to the French painter Christian Lemesle.

title: Queer art

encoding_log.content:
Title: Queer art

Queer art, also known as LGBT+ art or queer aesthetics, broadly refers to modern and contemporary visual art practices that draw on lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and other non-heterosexual or non-cisgender imagery and issues. By definition there can be no single, unified category of "queer art", because it encompasses a wide range of identities, contexts, and artistic approaches. 

However, contemporary artists who identify their practices as queer often call upon utopian and dystopian alternatives to ordinary life, adopt outlaw stances, embrace criminality and opacity, and forge unprecedented kinships and relationships. Queer art can be explicitly about sex and the embracing of unauthorised desires, challenging norms around sexuality and gender. Queer art is highly site-specific, with practices emerging very differently depending on context. 

In some places, queer artistic expression is advocated for and celebrated, while in others it is met with backlash, censorship, or even criminalisation. Because sex and gender operate differently in various national, religious, and ethnic contexts, queer art necessarily takes on varied meanings across cultures. Historically, the term "queer" functioned as a homophobic slur, particularly visible during the AIDS crisis in the United States in the 1980s. Since then, it has been re-appropriated and embraced by queer activists and integrated into many English-speaking academic and cultural contexts. 

As a result, international art practices by LGBT+ individuals are often placed under the umbrella term "queer art" in English-language discourse, even when they emerge outside the specific historical developments of U.S. gender and identity politics from the 1980s. The label "queer art" has also been used retroactively to describe the historic work of LGBT+ artists who practiced before present-day terminology such as lesbian, gay, bisexual, and trans was recognised. An example is the 2017 Tate exhibition "Queer British Art 1861–1967", which gathered works by artists whose lives and themes are now read through queer perspectives. 

The term "queer" is situated in the politics of non-normative gay, lesbian, and bisexual communities, though it is not equivalent to any of these categories and remains a fluid identity. Queer art adheres to no particular style or medium. It can take the form of performance art, video art, installation, drawing, painting, sculpture, photography, film, glass, and mixed media, among many other formats. 

Art historian Alex Pilcher, in "A Queer Little History of Art", notes that across art history, biographical information about queer artists has often been omitted or downplayed, or interpreted under the assumption of heterosexual identity. Same-sex partners might be described merely as "close friends", and artistic comrades recast as heterosexual love interests. Gay artists have historically been diagnosed in the record as celibate, asexual, or sexually confused, obscuring the queer dimensions of their lives and work. 

During the interwar period, there was greater acceptance of queer individuals in certain artistic urban centres such as Paris and Berlin. In 1920s New York, speakeasies in Harlem and Greenwich Village welcomed gay and lesbian clients, and cafés and bars across Europe and Latin America hosted artistic groups in which gay men could be integrated into mainstream cultural developments. Even in these more permissive environments, artists often developed visual codes to signify queerness covertly. 

Art historian Jonathan David Katz has written about Agnes Martin's abstract paintings as a form of queer self-realisation, suggesting that the tense, unreconciled equilibrium in works such as "Night Sea" (1963) reflects her identity as a closeted lesbian. Katz has also interpreted the iconography in Robert Rauschenberg's combine paintings, such as the inclusion of a picture of Judy Garland in "Bantam" (1954) and references to the myth of Ganymede in "Canyon" (1959), as allusions to Rauschenberg's identity as a gay man. 

Considering Rauschenberg's relationship with Jasper Johns, art historian Andrew Graham-Dixon reads Johns's monochrome encaustic painting "White Flag" (1955) in relation to Johns's experiences as a gay man in a repressive American society.

Title: Tamuri Wigness

Tamuri Slim Wigness Jr., born on 26 March 2002, is an Australian professional basketball player who most recently played for the North Gold Coast Seahawks in the NBL1 North. He was born in the Torres Strait Islands region of Queensland, Australia, and is of Indigenous Australian (Muralag) heritage.

At an early age, he moved with his family to Cairns, Queensland, where he began his primary schooling. While living in Cairns, his first sporting interest was junior rugby league, which he played until the age of 10. His mother then suggested he switch to basketball because it involved less physical contact, and he followed her advice.

Within a year of taking up basketball, Wigness joined Cairns Basketball's Tiny Taipans development program, which provided structured training and exposure to higher levels of the sport. At just 11 years old, he was given the opportunity to train with professional players from the Cairns Taipans, a National Basketball League (NBL) team.

During his teenage years, he attended Cairns State High School. While in high school, he continued to develop as a basketball player but also played junior Australian rules football with the Manunda Hawks in the local AFL Cairns competition. His performances in Australian rules football led to selection in multiple junior representative teams.

As a promising dual-sport athlete, Wigness drew interest from professional talent scouts. Along with fellow Cairns junior basketball standout Alex Davies, he was scouted by the Gold Coast Suns, an Australian Football League (AFL) club. Both players were offered places in the Suns' developmental academy. Davies accepted the offer and pursued a career in football, while Wigness chose to focus on basketball, declining the AFL pathway. Despite their different sporting directions, the two remained close friends and often trained together in both sports when they were based in the same area.

Wigness emerged as a leading junior basketball player in Queensland. At 14 years of age, he represented Queensland at the 2016 under-16 national championships. He starred throughout the tournament, averaging 25.56 points per game, and produced a standout performance by scoring 45 points in a game against South Australia.

In 2017, he accepted an NBA Global Academy scholarship, which granted him access to first-class training facilities at the Australian Institute of Sport complex in Canberra. That same year, he again represented Queensland at the under-16 national championships. His dominant play at state level led to his selection for the Australian national team at the 2017 FIBA Under-16 Asian Championship. There, he played a pivotal role in helping Australia win the gold medal and was named the starting point guard in the tournament's All-Tournament Team.

In 2018, Wigness travelled to Treviso, Italy, to participate in the NBA Global Camp. At this event, he impressed international scouts, forming an athletic backcourt combination with fellow Australian guard Josh Green.

Wigness continued to represent Australia in junior international competitions. He was part of the gold medal-winning Australian teams at the 2018 FIBA Under-18 Asian Championship and the 2019 FIBA Oceania Under-18 Championship. He also competed for Australia at the 2018 FIBA Under-17 Basketball World Cup and the 2019 FIBA Under-19 Basketball World Cup.

From 2017 to 2020, Wigness attended and played for the Basketball Australia Centre of Excellence, competing in the SEABL, NBL1, and Waratah League. During the 2019 NBL1 season, he averaged 11.7 points, four assists, and 3.4 rebounds per game, and in his season finale he recorded 22 points and 12 assists.

In 2019 he also travelled to Charlotte, North Carolina, to compete in the Basketball Without Borders Global Camp, where he again caught the attention of college and NBA scouts and earned All-Tournament honours.

title: Luce Turnier

encoding_log.content:
Title: Luce Turnier

Luce Turnier (February 24, 1924 – 1994) was a Haitian painter and collage artist who became one of Haiti’s leading modernist figures. She was born in 1924 in Jacmel, a town in southern Haiti. In 1937 a devastating hurricane struck southern Haiti, prompting her family to relocate to the capital, Port-au-Prince. This move later proved important for her artistic development, as Port-au-Prince became the center of a growing Haitian art movement.

Turnier began painting in 1944, at the age of 21, when she enrolled at Le Centre d’Art in Port-au-Prince. She soon became one of the founding members of this art school and gallery, which would play a central role in the emergence of modern Haitian art. As a young artist she admired the work of Brazilian painter Cândido Portinari and German artist Käthe Kollwitz, though she later explained that she grew out of these early influences as she developed her own style.

In a 1983 interview, Turnier described her training at Le Centre d’Art, noting that students started with still life and figure drawing, working from nude models and arranged objects. On Saturdays they went outdoors to paint landscapes, giving students a range of both studio and open-air experience.

Turnier belonged to Haiti’s middle class, as did Marie-Josée Nadal and Rose-Marie Desruisseaux, the other founding female artists at Le Centre d’Art. Their social status gave them access to artistic education, but middle-class Haitian society of the time did not encourage women to pursue careers in the arts. Women who persisted in artistic work were often stigmatized as deviants. Turnier recalled that although many women visited the Centre for a class or two, only about four or five women attended regularly in those early years. She also remembered the disdainful attitude of the Haitian bourgeoisie, who initially regarded the Centre’s artists as if they were “hippies” or “punks.”

Her paintings were featured in Studio No. 3, Le Centre d’Art’s monthly magazine. Turnier and a constellation of associated artists, including Albert Mangonès, Gérald Bloncourt, Maurice Borno, Rigaud Benoit, Hector Hyppolite, Daniel Lafontant, and others, formed the core of what became known as the Haitian Art Movement. The period from 1946 to 1950, which overlapped with the early phase of her career, is sometimes called “The Haitian Renaissance,” reflecting the vitality and innovation of Haitian visual arts at the time.

In 1946, with support from UNESCO, Turnier’s works were exhibited at the Musée d’Art Moderne de Paris, signaling her early international recognition. From December 8, 1949 until June 1950, her "Self-Portrait" was shown in the fine arts pavilion at the International Bi-Centennial Celebration of Port-au-Prince. In 1950 she and fellow artist Lucien Price helped to found an art gallery called The Foyer, further strengthening the institutional base for Haitian artists.

During the early 1950s, both the French and Haitian governments awarded Turnier scholarships to study abroad in the United States and Europe. She exhibited her work in Europe and studied in New York City and Paris. In New York she attended the Art Students League, where she became immersed in modernist theory that rejected traditional spatial illusionism and insisted on preserving the flatness of the picture plane.

Throughout this period she struggled to develop a personal style that integrated her Haitian heritage without surrendering to market expectations about what Haitian art should look like. She resisted stereotypical images favored by collectors who wanted exotic or folkloric themes, such as overt references to Haitian folklore and Vodou.

Turnier’s personal life intersected with her artistic trajectory. In 1954 she married the Italian painter Eugenio Carpi de Resmini, and the couple had two children. In 1965 she remarried, this time to the French painter Christian Lemesle.

title: Florence Warfield Sillers

encoding_log.content:
Title: Florence Warfield Sillers

Florence Carson Warfield Sillers was an American socialite and historian who became a prominent figure in Mississippi society. She was born on September 25, 1869, in Boonville, Missouri, and spent her childhood in Louisiana and Mississippi. Her parents were Colonel Elisha Warfield and Mary Anderson Carson. Her father was a planter who owned a plantation in Bolivar County, Mississippi, near the town of Rosedale. During the American Civil War he served as a Confederate officer in the 2nd Arkansas Infantry Regiment. Through him, Sillers was connected to a long-established American family with colonial roots. Sillers’s paternal ancestors had emigrated from Great Britain to the Province of Maryland in the seventeenth century. Among her notable relatives was her great-grandfather, also named Elisha Warfield, who was a physician and horse breeder. She was also a grandniece of Mary Jane Warfield Clay, who was known as a suffragist. These family connections linked her both to early colonial settlers and to later political and social activism.

In 1887, at the age of seventeen, Florence Warfield married Walter Sillers, a lawyer and member of a prominent Mississippi Delta family. She was his second wife. The couple had six children: Anna Farrar Sillers, Mary Sillers Skinner, Florence Sillers Ogden, Walter Sillers Jr., Evelyn Sillers Pearson, and Lillian Burrill Sillers Holleman. Her husband owned several plantations in Bolivar County and was active in state politics as a member of the Mississippi Democratic executive committee. The family lived in a Victorian-style mansion on Levee Street in Rosedale, Mississippi, which served as a base for their social and civic activities.

As a leading society figure in Mississippi, Florence Warfield Sillers belonged to numerous social, civic, and lineage organizations. She participated in local chapters of the Colonial Dames of America, an organization for women descended from prominent figures in the American colonies. She was also involved with the American Farm Bureau Federation and the American Red Cross, reflecting her interests in agriculture and public service. In addition, she took part in the activities of the Mississippi Delta Council and the Rosedale Country Club, groups that brought together influential residents of the region.

Religion and philanthropy played an important role in her public life. Sillers was a member of the Methodist Episcopal Church and devoted considerable time to charitable work. For twenty years she served as treasurer of the King’s Daughters Hospital of Rosedale, handling financial matters for the institution. Her historical interests were reflected in her membership in both the Texas State Historical Association and the Mississippi Historical Society, indicating her engagement with regional and state history beyond purely social pursuits.

A significant part of her identity was tied to lineage and historical societies. She was a founding member of the Mississippi Delta Chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution, an organization for women descended from individuals who contributed to American independence. Within this chapter she later served as regent, a leadership role responsible for guiding the group’s activities. She also joined the National Society Magna Charta Dames and Barons, an association for descendants of signers of the Magna Carta, further emphasizing her interest in hereditary connections to historical events and figures.

Sillers became known not only as a socialite but also as a writer of local history. In 1948 she published a book titled "History of Bolivar County, Mississippi." This work examined the history of Bolivar County but did so from a perspective that glorified the Confederacy and idealized the antebellum South. The book contributed to the Lost Cause narrative, a view of the Civil War and the Confederacy that sought to portray the Southern cause in a sympathetic and romanticized light.

Florence Carson Warfield Sillers lived until April 5, 1958, when she died in Mississippi. She was buried in Beulah Cemetery in Beulah, Mississippi. Over the course of her long life, she combined the roles of planter’s daughter, plantation owner’s wife, mother of six children, society leader, and amateur historian. Her many affiliations with historical, civic, and lineage societies, her prominent place in Mississippi social circles, and her authorship of a county history that promoted the Lost Cause interpretation of the Civil War together define her historical legacy as a representative of elite white Southern culture in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

Facebook, Inc. v. Duguid, 592 U.S. ___ (2021), was a United States Supreme Court case concerning how to interpret the term "automatic telephone dialing system" under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act of 1991 (TCPA). The dispute arose over whether Facebook’s security-alert text messaging system qualified as an autodialer under the statute and thus could expose the company to liability for sending unsolicited text messages.

The TCPA was enacted in 1991 to reduce the growing number of unsolicited calls consumers were receiving. Among its provisions, the law restricted the use of automated telephone dialing systems, often called autodialers, to contact consumers on services that might cost the recipient money, including cell phones and text messaging. Violations of these restrictions could be investigated and fined by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC).

Over time, Congress amended the TCPA. One important amendment, adopted in 2015, created an exception that allowed automated calls to numbers associated with services that charge the called party, when those calls were made to collect debts owed to or guaranteed by the federal government.

Since the law’s enactment, the TCPA’s autodialer restrictions have been challenged on First Amendment grounds, with plaintiffs arguing that the statute impermissibly restricted speech. Federal courts of appeals generally upheld the statute, finding it consistent with free speech protections.

The 2015 amendment, however, introduced a new constitutional argument. By exempting automated calls for federal debt collection, the law appeared to favor one type of speech over others, potentially making the autodialer restriction a content-based regulation of speech and therefore more vulnerable under the First Amendment.

At the same time that Facebook, Inc. v. Duguid was proceeding, another case, Barr v. American Association of Political Consultants, Inc., was advancing toward the Supreme Court to address whether this 2015 amendment rendered the autodialer provisions unconstitutional.

The factual dispute in Facebook, Inc. v. Duguid began in 2014, when Noah Duguid started receiving text messages on his cell phone from Facebook. These messages warned him of suspicious activity on a Facebook account, but Duguid did not have a Facebook account at all.

After attempting unsuccessfully to get Facebook to stop the messages, Duguid filed a class-action lawsuit in March 2015 in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California. He alleged that Facebook had violated the TCPA’s autodialer provision by using an automatic telephone dialing system (ATDS) to send him unwanted text messages.

Facebook moved to dismiss the lawsuit on two main grounds. First, it argued that its login or security notification system was not an ATDS because it did not generate phone numbers randomly or sequentially; instead, it sent targeted messages to specific numbers associated with particular user accounts or entries in a database. Second, Facebook challenged the constitutionality of the TCPA’s autodialer provision as modified by the 2015 amendment, contending that the law had become a content-based restriction on speech that violated the First Amendment.

Because the case now raised a constitutional question, the federal government intervened to defend the TCPA and support dismissal.

Title: Mykhailo Radutskyi

Mykhailo Borysovych Radutskyi is a Ukrainian entrepreneur, social activist, and politician who has served as a People's Deputy of Ukraine in multiple convocations of the Verkhovna Rada, the country’s national parliament. He was born on 5 December 1968 in Kyiv, the capital of Ukraine. His educational background combines medical training and sports science. Radutskyi studied at the P. I. Gavros Kyiv Medical College, where he qualified as an Emergency Medical Technician. He later continued his education at the National University of Ukraine on Physical Education and Sport, specializing in Olympic and professional sport. At this institution he received a master’s degree in Olympic and professional sport.

Early in his career Radutskyi worked directly in the medical field. In 1987 he served as an Emergency Medical Technician at a Kyiv ambulance station, applying his medical college training to emergency healthcare. After this period in frontline medical service, his professional path shifted toward management and the cultural sector. From 1989 to 1993 he held the position of deputy director of an organization called "Kyivconcert." This role marked the beginning of his experience in administration and leadership.

In 1993 Radutskyi entered the medical business. Over the following decade he built a career as a manager in a private medical company. From 1994 to 2004 he served as commercial director and then deputy director of the limited liability company "Boris." In 2004 he became president of LLC "Boris," reflecting his growing influence and responsibility in the private healthcare sector. His work there connected his early medical training with entrepreneurial activity and healthcare management.

Radutskyi also became active in broader medical governance. At some point he was a member of the Higher Medical Council of the Ministry of Healthcare of Ukraine, indicating his involvement in national-level medical policy or advisory work. His role extended beyond the private sector into public and professional health structures.

In 2015 he moved further into public service when he became an advisor to the head of the Kyiv City State Administration, Vitali Klitschko. This advisory role placed him in the municipal executive sphere of Ukraine’s capital city.

By 2019 Radutskyi had become an important figure in national politics. He was nominated as a candidate for People’s Deputy from the political party Servant of the People for the 2019 parliamentary elections. He appeared as number 18 on the party list, indicating a high position among the party’s candidates, although he himself was formally non-partisan and not a registered member of any party.

On 30 July 2019 President Volodymyr Zelensky appointed him as an out-of-state advisor to the president, further demonstrating the trust placed in him by the country’s leadership.

In the 2019 Ukrainian parliamentary elections Radutskyi was elected a People’s Deputy of Ukraine of the ninth convocation as number 18 on the Servant of the People party list. In parliament he joined the Servant of the People parliamentary faction. Within the Verkhovna Rada he took on a key committee role as Chairperson of the Committee on Public Health, Medical Assistance and Medical Insurance, aligning his legislative work with his professional experience in healthcare.

Radutskyi also became active in interparliamentary cooperation. He served as a member of the Ukrainian part of the interparliamentary assembly that includes the parliament of Georgia, the parliament of the Republic of Moldova, and the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine. In addition, he was a deputy member of the Ukrainian part of the Parliamentary Association Committee.

He headed several groups for inter-parliamentary relations, including those with the Kingdom of Thailand and with the Republic of Moldova. He was also head of a group for inter-parliamentary relations with Moldova, and a member of groups maintaining relations with the Italian Republic, the Republic of Kazakhstan, the Republic of Armenia, the French Republic, and the Republic of Croatia.

Title: Tamuri Wigness

Tamuri Slim Wigness Jr., born on 26 March 2002, is an Australian professional basketball player who most recently played for the North Gold Coast Seahawks in the NBL1 North. He was born in the Torres Strait Islands region of Queensland, Australia, and is of Indigenous Australian (Muralag) heritage.

At an early age, he moved with his family to Cairns, Queensland, where he began his primary schooling. While living in Cairns, his first sporting interest was junior rugby league, which he played until the age of 10. His mother then suggested he switch to basketball because it involved less physical contact, and he followed her advice.

Within a year of taking up basketball, Wigness joined Cairns Basketball's Tiny Taipans development program, which provided structured training and exposure to higher levels of the sport. At just 11 years old, he was given the opportunity to train with professional players from the Cairns Taipans, a National Basketball League (NBL) team.

During his teenage years, he attended Cairns State High School. While in high school, he continued to develop as a basketball player but also played junior Australian rules football with the Manunda Hawks in the local AFL Cairns competition. His performances in Australian rules football led to selection in multiple junior representative teams.

As a promising dual-sport athlete, Wigness drew interest from professional talent scouts. Along with fellow Cairns junior basketball standout Alex Davies, he was scouted by the Gold Coast Suns, an Australian Football League (AFL) club. Both players were offered places in the Suns' developmental academy. Davies accepted the offer and pursued a career in football, while Wigness chose to focus on basketball, declining the AFL pathway. Despite their different sporting directions, the two remained close friends and often trained together in both sports when they were based in the same area.

Wigness emerged as a leading junior basketball player in Queensland. At 14 years of age, he represented Queensland at the 2016 under-16 national championships. He starred throughout the tournament, averaging 25.56 points per game, and produced a standout performance by scoring 45 points in a game against South Australia.

In 2017, he accepted an NBA Global Academy scholarship, which granted him access to first-class training facilities at the Australian Institute of Sport complex in Canberra. That same year, he again represented Queensland at the under-16 national championships. His dominant play at state level led to his selection for the Australian national team at the 2017 FIBA Under-16 Asian Championship. There, he played a pivotal role in helping Australia win the gold medal and was named the starting point guard in the tournament's All-Tournament Team.

In 2018, Wigness travelled to Treviso, Italy, to participate in the NBA Global Camp. At this event, he impressed international scouts, forming an athletic backcourt combination with fellow Australian guard Josh Green.

Wigness continued to represent Australia in junior international competitions. He was part of the gold medal-winning Australian teams at the 2018 FIBA Under-18 Asian Championship and the 2019 FIBA Oceania Under-18 Championship. He also competed for Australia at the 2018 FIBA Under-17 Basketball World Cup and the 2019 FIBA Under-19 Basketball World Cup.

From 2017 to 2020, Wigness attended and played for the Basketball Australia Centre of Excellence, competing in the SEABL, NBL1, and Waratah League. During the 2019 NBL1 season, he averaged 11.7 points, four assists, and 3.4 rebounds per game, and in his season finale he recorded 22 points and 12 assists.

In 2019 he also travelled to Charlotte, North Carolina, to compete in the Basketball Without Borders Global Camp, where he again caught the attention of college and NBA scouts and earned All-Tournament honours.
